## Installation

### "could not find tools necessary to compile a package" / install fails

`fast.string` compiles C++ source on install (PCRE2 bindings, prepared
literal search, RcppParallel). You need a working toolchain:

- **Windows**: install [Rtools](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/)
  matching your R version, and make sure it's on `PATH` (the Rtools
  installer offers to do this). Verify with
  `pkgbuild::has_build_tools(debug = TRUE)`.
- **macOS**: install Xcode command-line tools (`xcode-select --install`)
  and PCRE2 (`brew install pcre2`).
- **Linux**: a C++ compiler (gcc/clang) plus the PCRE2 development
  headers — `libpcre2-dev` on Debian/Ubuntu, `pcre2-devel` on
  Fedora/RHEL.

fast.string needs R 4.1.0 or later.

If `pkgbuild::has_build_tools(debug = TRUE)` returns `FALSE`, the
underlying compiler invocation it prints is the fastest way to see exactly
what's missing.

### Reinstalling after pulling new source changes

If you're developing against a local checkout rather than installing a
release, `devtools::load_all()` recompiles changed `src/*.cpp` files
automatically; a plain `library(fast.string)` won't pick up source changes
without reinstalling first.

## NA, empty strings, and encoding

### Why does my function return `NA` for a non-`NA` input?

Every function in this package returns `NA` for `NA` input — but a few
functions also return `NA` for specific *valid-looking but unparseable*
inputs:

- `soundex()`/`nysiis()`/`refined_soundex()`/`double_metaphone()` return
  `NA` for strings with **no alphabetic characters at all** (e.g. `"123"`,
  `""`) — there's no phonetic code for a string with nothing to encode
  phonetically. `cologne()` does the same, counting umlauts and `ß` as
  letters it can encode. `caverphone()` is the exception: it always returns
  a 10-character code for non-`NA` input (even `""`, which codes as
  `"1111111111"`), matching its reference implementation's behaviour.
- `fas.Date()` returns `NA` for any string that doesn't match the
  specified `format` *exactly* (wrong length, wrong separator position,
  non-digit where a digit is expected) or has an out-of-range month/day.
  Unlike `base::as.Date()`, it does **not** attempt multiple formats or
  partial parsing.
- `fas.POSIXct()` is stricter still: on top of the same exact-shape rule,
  it validates the **whole calendar**, so `"2023-02-29 00:00:00"` is `NA`
  even though every field is individually in range. This is deliberate and
  is the one place the timestamp functions are less permissive than the
  date functions — see @sec-theory.

```{r}
soundex(c("Smith", "123", "", NA))
fas.Date(c("2024-06-18", "2024/06/18", "2024-13-01"), "iso")  # 2nd: wrong separator, 3rd: month 13
fas.POSIXct(c("2024-06-18 09:15:00", "2023-02-29 00:00:00"))  # 2nd: not a leap year
```

### `fchartr()` silently fell back to `base::chartr()` — why?

`fchartr()`'s fast path is a flat 256-entry byte lookup table, which only
works correctly when every character in `old` and `new` is single-byte
(ASCII). If either argument contains a multi-byte UTF-8 character (an
accented letter, a curly quote, an emoji), the function detects that via
a byte-count vs. char-count comparison and transparently delegates to
`base::chartr()` instead — same result, just without the speedup, and
without you needing to know in advance.

```{r}
fchartr("e", "é", "test")  # "é" is multi-byte — falls back to base::chartr(), still correct
```

### `fnchar()` bytes vs. chars

`type = "bytes"` counts bytes; `type = "chars"` counts Unicode codepoints.
These differ for any non-ASCII input — get this backwards and a
fixed-width field extraction (`fsubstr()`) on multi-byte data will be off
by however many multi-byte characters are in the string.

```{r}
fnchar("café", type = "bytes")  # 5 — "é" is 2 bytes in UTF-8
fnchar("café", type = "chars") # 4 — 4 visible characters
```

### Similarity bytes vs. Unicode code points

Established edit-distance and Jaro-Winkler functions default to
`use_bytes = TRUE` for compatibility. Set `use_bytes = FALSE` when one
accented character or emoji should count as one comparison symbol. Fuzzy
lookup defaults to code points. This does not perform Unicode normalization:
precomposed and decomposed spellings can still compare differently.

Bytes-encoded R strings cannot be decoded as Unicode and produce an indexed
error in code-point mode; pass `use_bytes = TRUE` when those bytes are the
intended data.

## Threading

### Does `nthreads` affect later calls?

No. Functions that expose `nthreads` pass it to the native dispatcher as a
**per-call cap**; they do not change RcppParallel's process-wide options.
`NULL` uses the RcppParallel default for that call, a positive integer
limits it to at most that many threads, and `nthreads = 1` forces strict
serial execution. A later call without `nthreads` is unaffected.

The dispatcher can use fewer threads than the cap when the input contains
too little useful work. String-utility, date, and phonetic functions keep
their existing signatures and use the default scheduler for their own
calls.

### Does `nthreads` help on a machine with few cores?

Not much below 4 cores, and the package's own size thresholds
(@sec-theory) mean it won't even try to parallelise small inputs
regardless. If you're running inside a container with a CPU limit lower
than `parallel::detectCores()` reports (common in CI and some cloud
environments), set `nthreads` explicitly to the actual limit — TBB doesn't
know about cgroup CPU quotas and will otherwise oversubscribe.

The supported Windows build always uses TBB. On a diagnostic build forced
to RcppParallel's TinyThread backend, values above one are advisory because
that backend ignores the native thread-count argument; the dispatcher
coarsens its ranges to limit useful parallel work instead. `nthreads = 1`
still runs strictly serially on either backend. Set the build variable
`FAST_STRING_TINYTHREAD=1` only when installing such a diagnostic build.

## Performance

### Which functions are *not* faster than base R?

Several, and it is better to know which than to find out. Every function
here pays a fixed cost per call that base R does not: it copies the
vector's string pointers into a snapshot the worker threads can read
safely, plans the work into byte-balanced chunks, and assembles the
result. When the actual work is one cheap pass over short strings, that
scaffolding is most of the cost, and base R's own C code is already near
the floor.

```{r}
#| label: slower-than-base
set.seed(1)
n <- 5e5
# Short values with a handful of matches each: names, codes, postcodes.
x <- vapply(seq_len(4000),
            function(i) paste(sample(LETTERS, 8, TRUE), collapse = ""), "")
x <- sample(x, n, TRUE)

ms <- function(f, reps = 5) {
    f(); start <- Sys.time()
    for (i in seq_len(reps)) f()
    round(1000 * (as.numeric(Sys.time()) - as.numeric(start)) / reps, 1)
}
cmp <- function(label, fast, base) {
    f <- ms(fast); b <- ms(base)
    data.frame(operation = label, fast_ms = f, base_ms = b,
               ratio = round(b / f, 2))
}
do.call(rbind, list(
    cmp("substr(), positive positions",
        function() fsubstr(x, 1, 4), function() substr(x, 1, 4)),
    cmp("substr(), from the end",
        function() fsubstr(x, -3, -1),
        function() substring(x, nchar(x) - 2, nchar(x))),
    cmp("strsplit() to a list",
        function() fstrsplit(x, "A"), function() strsplit(x, "A", fixed = TRUE)),
    cmp("one field of a split",
        function() fsplit_field(x, "A", 1),
        function() vapply(strsplit(x, "A", fixed = TRUE), `[`, "", 1L)),
    cmp("grepl(), fixed, 8 characters",
        function() fgrepl("A", x, fixed = TRUE),
        function() grepl("A", x, fixed = TRUE)),
    cmp("gsub(), fixed, 8 characters",
        function() fgsub("A", "4", x, fixed = TRUE),
        function() gsub("A", "4", x, fixed = TRUE)),
    cmp("gsub(), regular expression",
        function() fgsub("[AEIOU]", "", x),
        function() gsub("[AEIOU]", "", x)),
    cmp("grepl(), regular expression",
        function() fgrepl("^[A-M].*N$", x),
        function() grepl("^[A-M].*N$", x))
))
```

Read `ratio` as "times faster than base R"; below 1 means base R wins.
The pattern, which holds across machines even though the exact numbers do
not:

- **`fsubstr()` with plain positive positions is slower than `substr()`**,
  which already does one cheap pass. It wins decisively on *negative*
  positions — `fsubstr(x, -3, -1)` for the last three characters —
  where the base R equivalent needs an `nchar()` call and arithmetic per
  element.
- **`fstrsplit()` is slower than `strsplit()`.** The cost is building half
  a million R character vectors, which happens on the main thread either
  way. If you only want one field, `fsplit_field()` skips the list
  entirely and beats `strsplit()` plus `vapply()` several times over —
  that is the function to reach for.
- **Fixed-string matching and substitution on short values is roughly a
  tie**, and which way it falls depends on how many elements actually
  contain the pattern. When most do not match, base R returns them
  untouched almost for free while this package still pays for the
  snapshot; when most do, the parallel substitution pulls ahead. Neither
  direction is worth restructuring code for.
- **Regular expressions are where the package wins**, and the margin grows
  with the length of the subject and the complexity of the pattern,
  because PCRE2 matching is the part that parallelises.

Two more cases where base R is the better tool:

- **Short vectors.** Below a few thousand elements nothing parallelises
  (the thresholds are in @sec-theory) and the per-call cost dominates.
  These functions are for columns, not scalars.
- **Scalar calls inside a loop.** Call them once on the whole vector.

None of this applies to the functions with no base R equivalent — the
phonetic codes, the similarity metrics, `fcount()`, `format_date()`,
`fas.Date()`, `freplace_tokens()`, `string_shape()`, `fpad()`,
`freverse()`, `rLink()`. There the comparison is against a hand-written
loop or another package, the gaps are one to two orders of magnitude, and
@sec-benchmarks makes it.

### `rLink()` is slower than I expected — where is the time going?

Read `attr(result, "timings")`. It breaks the call into the stages that
scale differently: `keys` is work per *record* (phonetic codes, date
formatting, joining the terms of each key), `pairs` is the blocking itself,
`attach` is copying the carried columns onto the pairs, and one row per
comparator is work per *candidate pair*.

```{r}
#| label: rlink-timings-faq
people <- data.frame(
    given    = sample(c("JOHN", "MARY", "ROBERT"), 2e4, TRUE),
    surname  = sample(c("SMITH", "JONES", "NGUYEN", "PATEL"), 2e4, TRUE),
    dob      = as.Date("1950-01-01") + sample(0:2e4, 2e4, TRUE),
    postcode = sprintf("%04d", sample(3000:3100, 2e4, TRUE)))
r <- rLink(people, block = list(list(soundex(surname), dob)),
           compare = list(jaro_winkler(given)), keep = character())
attr(r, "timings")
```

If `keys` dominates, the blocking expressions are the cost: a term written
into several passes is evaluated once per side, so that is already shared,
but an expensive one (`daitch_mokotoff()`, `ngram_fingerprint()`) is worth
computing into a column beforehand. If a *comparator* dominates, there are
too many candidate pairs — tighten the key or set
`max_block_size`, and check `attr(result, "compare")` to be sure a
comparator is not being applied to a column you did not mean. If `attach`
dominates, pass `keep` to carry fewer columns, or `keep = character()` to
carry none and join back by the indices.

## Regex behaviour

### `fsub()`/`fgsub()` with `perl = FALSE` replaced a different match than base R

Where alternatives can match at the same position, base R's default (TRE)
engine takes the *longest* match and PCRE2 takes the *first* alternative
that matches: `sub("a|ab", "X", "abc")` gives `"Xc"`, `fsub()` gives
`"Xbc"`. Whether something matches (`fgrepl()`) is unaffected. List the
longer alternative first (`"ab|a"`) to get the same result from both.
Everything else about `perl = FALSE` follows base R's rules -- see
@sec-theory.

Patterns that only PCRE understands (lookarounds, atomic groups,
possessive quantifiers, named groups) run with `perl = TRUE` semantics even
when `perl = FALSE`, still on the fast path. `fcount()` delegates only an
empty `pattern` to `base::gregexpr()`, because base R counts those matches
in characters.

### A warning says "PCRE2 error 'match limit exceeded' for element ..."

The pattern backtracked too much on that element (see the next question).
As in base R, that element counts as not matching -- `FALSE` for
`fgrepl()`, unchanged for `fsub()`/`fgsub()`, `0` for `fcount()` -- and the
rest of the vector is processed normally.

### Catastrophic backtracking — am I safe?

Only partially. The prepared `fixed = TRUE` path treats the pattern as
literal bytes, so regex backtracking cannot occur. PCRE2 (used for general
regex) is **not** immune — it's still a backtracking engine, in the same
risk class as base R's `perl = TRUE`. If you're matching untrusted patterns
against untrusted input, that risk exists regardless of which package you
use; this package doesn't add to it, but doesn't remove it either. Prefer
`fixed = TRUE` whenever the pattern is actually a literal string: it avoids
regex backtracking and is also the fastest path in the package.

- Found a bug, or a discrepancy between `fast.string` and base R's
  behaviour on some input? Open an issue:
